core_summary: This chapter investigates the fundamental properties of magnets, distinguishing magnetic from non-magnetic materials. It details magnetic poles (North and South), the directive property of freely suspended magnets, compass construction, single-touch magnetisation, and the fundamental law of attraction and repulsion.
key_concepts: Classification of materials into Magnetic (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) and Non-magnetic (wood, plastic, copper, rubber).
Poles of a Magnet: Magnetic force is concentrated at the North and South poles and weakest at the center.
Directive Property: A freely suspended magnet aligns along Earth's North-South magnetic axis.
Laws of Magnetism: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Repulsion is the only sure test for magnetism.
Demagnetization: Magnets lose strength when heated, hammered, dropped, or improperly stored.

key_terms.definition: The two opposite ends of a magnet where magnetic attractive force is maximum.
A navigational device containing a pivoted magnetic needle that points toward Earth's geographic North-South direction.
An ancient Indian directional navigation device consisting of a magnetized iron fish floating in oil.

key_takeaways: Magnetic poles always exist in inseparable pairs (N and S).
Repulsion between two objects confirms that both objects are magnetized.
Proper handling and soft iron keepers protect magnets from losing their magnetism over time.
